thesis_statement: Regardless of how AI, crypto, currency, or inflation evolve, society always converges back to five basic-needs industries — Food, Water, Shelter, Education, Healthcare. AI should be treated as a tool serving these sectors, not as the investment target itself.
macro_context: AI diffuses broadly but gradually over ~10 years, concentrated in knowledge work (McKinsey: $2.6-4.4T annual value; Goldman: ~7% global GDP uplift, ~25% of US work hours automatable, 6-9% transitional worker displacement spread over a decade). US health spending grows to 19.7% of GDP by 2032; 65+ population grows ~1.6%/yr through 2036, 80+ population doubles 2015-2035, driving an 806,000-unit / $275B senior-housing supply gap by 2030. Stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets (incl. ~$5T of tokenized real estate) go mainstream under the GENIUS Act (2025), and inflation runs structurally stickier than the 2010s (IMF: 4.1%->4.4% 2025-26). Physical constraints (power, water, care labor, buildable senior-housing supply) become binding bottlenecks, not compute.
source_notes: Sub-scores derived from basic_needs_thesis_stress_test_report.md (research session 2026-07-20, Perplexity wide-search research subagent). Every score below traces to a cited source in that report; see `sources` per sector. Scores are the author's structured judgment applied to the cited evidence, not the report's own numbers restated -- re-derive if the underlying report is updated.

sectors.name: Food
exposed_sub_verticals: Conventional meat production (cultivated-meat cost parity path)
counter_thesis_notes: Food-at-home spending fell only 5.7% in the Great Recession and rose during COVID -- demand is inelastic, but food PRICES are among the most volatile CPI components (FAH inflation ranged -1.3% to +11.4%, 2016-2022) -- BLS excludes food from core inflation for this reason.

McKinsey: cultivated meat could reach cost parity with conventional meat by ~2030 (costs fell 99% in under a decade), though skeptical forecasts give only 8-16% probability of major retail/fast-food adoption by end-2031 -- disruption is real but slower than boosters claim, and it threatens commodity producers, not grocery demand itself.

sectors.name: Water
counter_thesis_notes: As a regulated UTILITY, water's public-equity expression fell -31.55% in 2008 -- worse than both Consumer Staples (-17.66%) and Health Care (-24.48%), though still better than the S&P (-38.49%). Regulated returns cap upside and rate-sensitivity hurts in downturns -- scarcity of the underlying resource does not equal low price volatility of the asset.
Water is climate-exposed on both sides: supply shocks (droughts, extreme weather) and desalination/efficiency tech on the supply-expansion side could alter the scarcity picture faster than assumed.

sectors.name: Shelter
resilient_sub_verticals: Needs-based senior housing (assisted living, memory care, RCFE)
counter_thesis_notes: Housing WAS the epicenter of the 2008 crash. Even senior housing -- the most demand-durable real-estate sub-vertical -- saw occupancy crater to a record-low 78.8% in Q1 2021 (down 8.7pp) with NOI falling double digits in 2020-21, though it recovered strongly by 2024 (87.2% occupancy, 19.5% NOI CAGR 2021-2024).

Healthcare real estate valuations fell 10-20% in the 2023-24 rate shock despite unchanged underlying demand -- proving leverage and rates dominate short-run asset behavior independent of demand durability.

BCG projects ~$5T of real estate tokenized by 2030; fractionalized, 24/7-tradable real estate could import crypto-market volatility and correlation into an asset class prized for its illiquidity premium.

sectors.name: Education
exposed_sub_verticals: Credential-based delivery models exposed to AI tutoring
counter_thesis_notes: Weakest link of the five sectors. A World Bank RCT of generative-AI tutoring in Nigeria produced ~0.3 SD learning gains -- equivalent to ~2 years of typical learning in 6 weeks -- a genuine substitution threat to the delivery layer of traditional education.

Demographic 'enrollment cliff' (falling birth rate) is already pushing college closures, and NBER research documents a flattening of the higher-education wage premium -- undermining the sector's traditional counter-cyclical enrollment pattern.
'Education' as a need survives; 'the education industry as currently structured' (four-year residential higher-ed) may not.

sectors.name: Healthcare
resilient_sub_verticals: Needs-based, real-asset-backed healthcare (senior housing, medical office, skilled nursing)
exposed_sub_verticals: Fee-for-service providers exposed to a value-based-care margin shift
counter_thesis_notes: AI's effect on healthcare COSTS is contested: credible analysis argues AI is likely to INCREASE total spending under fee-for-service (AI scribes -> more visits; AI-enabled remote monitoring -> more interventions), which is good for gross revenue but could compress provider margins if reimbursement shifts to value-based care.
Healthcare real estate valuations fell 10-20% in the 2023-24 rate shock even though fundamentals (occupancy, rents) stayed strong -- same leverage/rate risk as Shelter.

counter_thesis_points: 'Durable demand' is not the same as 'stable asset' -- every one of the five sectors has a real-asset or equity expression carrying leverage, rate, and liquidity risk independent of demand (senior housing occupancy crash 2020-21; healthcare RE -10-20% valuations in the 2023-24 rate shock).
Education is genuinely disintermediable: AI tutors + demographic enrollment cliff + flattening wage premium threaten the incumbent form of the sector even though the underlying need persists.
Food's commodity/agriculture layer can be restructured by cultivated meat and vertical farming, though grocery demand itself stays inelastic.
Tokenization (~$5T of real estate by 2030 per BCG) could make 'shelter as a stable asset' MORE volatile by importing crypto-market-like liquidity and correlation.
AI is a live cost-INCREASE risk in healthcare under fee-for-service, not a guaranteed cost-compression tailwind.
Water's utility-equity expression was MORE volatile than Staples/Healthcare in 2008 -- resource scarcity does not equal low asset-price volatility.

MIT 2025 study: ~95% of enterprise generative-AI pilots produced no measurable P&L impact -- this supports 'AI as tool not target' but also implies the AI-application layer itself is being rapidly commoditized, a distinct risk to an AI-agent business.

A front-loaded AI job-displacement shock (Goldman's aggressive scenario: up to ~15M US workers) would reduce household income and pressure demand even in basic-needs sectors; a stickier/higher inflation regime is a persistent headwind for rate-sensitive real assets regardless of sector.
